\paragraph{Shape is not rank.} Counting rows and columns gives only an upper bound on what can be fitted: an underdetermined shape guarantees an exact fit only if the matrix has full row rank. In Table~I the fits with more coefficients than levels (zeros 1--300 with $M=400$, 1--400 with $M=600$, 1--800 with $M=900$) still have in-sample rms $0.120$, $0.064$ and $0.103$. Sec.~III reports that the 500 zeros are reproduced to rms $<10^{-4}$ only by $M=900$, not as soon as $M$ exceeds 500. The linearized sensitivity matrix is therefore effectively rank deficient until the cosines can resolve the wavefunctions of the levels being fitted. This is the paper's coverage law $M\pi/L>2\sqrt E$, discussed in Chapter~\ref{ch:fitting}, and the notion of ``effectively'' rank deficient (tiny but nonzero singular values) is made precise in Chapter~\ref{ch:least-squares}.

patches.new: The geometry of \cref{eq:linear-algebra-beatnull} is consistent with the paper's two statements ``the held-out rms never improves on the null'' and ``no reproducible positive held-out correlation appears'' (Sec.~III) appearing together. When $\cos\theta$ is zero or negative, no nonzero prediction can beat the null. When $\cos\theta$ is small and positive, only a prediction of small amplitude, $\norm{\bm p}<2\norm{\bm d}\cos\theta$, can. This is a guide, not an exact explanation, for two reasons. The paper's corr is the centered (Pearson) cosine.
